title: Cockroach Milk, How to Blow Your Nose, and Mosquito Printers: The Ig Nobels of 2026
gist: Wired recaps the 2026 Ig Nobel Prizes, awarded in Zurich by Improbable Research, covering ten real-but-absurd-sounding studies — from turning dead mosquito proboscises into 3D-printer nozzles to research linking higher social class with more unethical behavior — that use humor to spotlight legitimate science.

insights.claim: Researchers won the Ig Nobel Prize in Technology for showing that a dead mosquito's proboscis can function as an extremely fine, ready-made nozzle for a 3D printer, since the proboscis is essentially an ultrathin needle evolved for piercing skin.
insights.speaker: Jorge Garay
insights.so_what: It's a concrete example of biomimicry replacing costly precision-machined components (printer nozzles) with an already-optimized biological structure, a pattern worth watching in low-cost manufacturing and materials research.
insights.quote: Evolution had already come up with a great solution by optimizing the mosquito’s mouthparts.
insights.locator: Prize in Technology: Dead Mosquitos Can Become 3D Printers

insights.claim: The price of 3D printers has fallen significantly over the past decade, to the point where the article frames a dead mosquito as a viable substitute for one of a printer's most delicate parts.
insights.speaker: Jorge Garay
insights.so_what: Reinforces the broader consumer/prosumer hardware trend of 3D printing commoditizing over the last decade.
insights.locator: Prize in Technology: Dead Mosquitos Can Become 3D Printers

insights.claim: A separate Ig Nobel-winning study found that lowering the impact angle of a liquid stream hitting a urinal significantly reduces splash-back, and researchers built prototype urinals based on that mathematical model.
insights.speaker: Jorge Garay
insights.so_what: A small but real example of applied fluid-dynamics modeling translating directly into a manufacturable product design (splash-reducing urinals) for public health/sanitation.
insights.locator: Prize in Physics: How to Make a Urinal Splash-Free

themes.theme: Human behavior and social science findings

insights.claim: A peer-reviewed study published in PNAS, titled 'Higher Social Class Predicts Increased Unethical Behavior,' ran seven experiments and found that people from higher socioeconomic classes are, on average, more likely to break traffic rules, fail to yield right of way, cheat, and even take candy meant for children.
insights.speaker: Jorge Garay
insights.so_what: A data point on how wealth/status correlates with self-interested rule-breaking — relevant context for behavioral-economics and governance/ESG discussions about elite conduct.
insights.quote: Higher Social Class Predicts Increased Unethical Behavior
insights.locator: Prize in Economics: Having More Money Might Make You a Bad Person

insights.claim: Researchers stepping on a venomous South American pit viper (Bothrops jararaca) while wearing a boot found bite probability varied sharply by body location: 44% when pressure was applied to the head, 20% to the body, and only 11% to the tail.
insights.speaker: Jorge Garay
insights.so_what: Not investable, but a concrete quantified risk finding of the kind the piece highlights as genuine science delivered with a comedic framing.
insights.locator: Prize in Biology: When Do Snakes Decide to Bite?

insights.claim: About 1,000 participants buried cotton underwear in soil and later measured decomposition to create an 'underwear index' — more holes indicate more cellulose-degrading microbial activity, a proxy for farmland soil health.
insights.speaker: Jorge Garay
insights.so_what: A genuinely low-cost, low-tech proxy method for assessing agricultural soil biology that could interest low-cost agri-testing approaches.
insights.locator: Prize in Soil Science: Old Underwear Can Reveal Soil Health
